name: November 1960 Great Storm

phenomena.details: Dst −339 nT, Kp 9; one of the most intense storms during Solar Cycle 19 (the historically most active cycle).
Multiple X-class flares from large active regions.
Major SEP event with high proton flux; GLE #8 and #9 on November 12 and 15, 1960.
Widespread shortwave radio blackouts across sunlit hemisphere.

impacts.description: Widespread disruption to telegraph, telephone, and early data communication lines due to geomagnetically induced currents; multiple days of degraded service.
Aurora widely visible across the continental United States and Europe; observers as far south as New Mexico and Arizona reported vivid displays.
Shortwave radio blackouts on the sunlit hemisphere for multiple hours during the peak X-class flares; polar cap absorption disrupted high-latitude communications for days.

papers.title: Solar and Terrestrial Relationships During the International Geophysical Year
papers.keyFinding: Comprehensive analysis of solar-terrestrial connections during 1957–1962, including the November 1960 storm complex during the highest sunspot maximum of the modern era.

summary: The November 1960 geomagnetic storm (Dst −339 nT, Kp 9) was one of the largest events of Solar Cycle 19 – the most active sunspot cycle in recorded history – causing widespread radio blackouts, communication disruptions, and aurora visible across the continental United States.
description: Solar Cycle 19 (peaked 1958) was the strongest cycle in the modern record with a smoothed sunspot maximum of 201.3. While the all-time peak had passed, the Sun remained highly active into late 1960. The November 1960 storm complex began with multiple X-class flares producing severe radio blackouts, followed by fast CMEs that drove a peak Dst of −339 nT and Kp 9 on November 13. Major solar energetic particle events (GLE #8 and #9, November 12 and 15) added an S4-class radiation storm. Telegraph and telephone communications in Canada and northern Europe were disrupted for days by GICs, while aurora reached latitudes of ~30°N in the United States. The event demonstrated the compounding hazard of multiple phenomena (flares, CMEs, SEPs) occurring in rapid succession during the declining phase of a strong solar cycle.
